vignette:
Mr. Tran speaks of his life in two distinct parts: before the river, and after. Before the river, he was a young man of twenty-eight in Saigon, a student of engineering with a quick smile, promised to a girl named Lien. He speaks of the scent of jasmine and street food, the drone of motorcycles, the oppressive humidity that was as familiar as his own skin. This part of his story is told in soft, almost wistful tones, a memory of a person he barely recognizes.

The second part of his life began in April of 1975. He doesn't describe the decision to flee as a choice, but as a current that swept his family along. The memory is not a linear story but a collection of sensory fragments that surface without warning. The crush of bodies at the docks, the suffocating smell of diesel fuel and human sweat. The high-pitched scream of a child, a sound he can still hear in the silence of his own home. His primary role, as he saw it, was to keep his hand clamped firmly on the wrist of his younger sister, Mai, a small, terrified girl of sixteen. He describes the chaotic push onto a dangerously overcrowded barge on the Saigon River. The sun was hot, the air thick with smoke from distant fires. He remembers the feeling of the boat listing, the collective gasp of the crowd, and the chilling finality of the helicopters chopping the air overhead. That is where the clear memory splinters. He remembers the shouting, the panic, but not the moment Mai’s wrist slipped from his grasp. He remembers being in the water, the oily taste of it, and seeing her face for a moment before she was gone.

He and Lien, who had been on a different boat, eventually made it to a refugee camp, and then to America. The guilt was a physical weight, a stone in his gut he carried everywhere. He needed to build a new life, but the old one was a constant, screaming ghost. He found work, but his nights were filled with the river. He would wake up gasping, his wife’s hand on his shoulder, the smell of smoke still in his nostrils. During the day, any loud noise—a car backfiring, a slammed door—would send a jolt of pure adrenaline through him, his hands clenching into fists.

He joined the fire department in his early thirties. It seemed, to his wife, like a strange choice for a man haunted by fire and chaos. But for Mr. Tran, it was the only thing that made sense. The uniform was armor. The blare of the siren was a sound he could control; it was a call to action, not a warning of incoming danger. He ran toward the fire, into the smoke, because in there, he had a purpose. He had an axe, a hose, and a team. He could save people. For thirty years, the controlled chaos of the firehouse was his sanctuary. The adrenaline of a call drowned out the intrusive memories of the river. The exhaustion after a 24-hour shift was the only thing that brought him dreamless sleep. He was a good firefighter, methodical and calm under pressure. He was saving other people’s sisters, other people’s families.

Retirement, five years ago, dismantled his fortress. The silence of his small suburban home is now more deafening than any siren. There are no bells to call him to action, no structure to contain the memories. He’ll be in his garden, tending his prize-winning roses, and the smell of a neighbor’s barbecue will suddenly become the oily smoke of 1975. He sits for hours in his armchair, staring at the television without seeing it, his mind replaying the moment the barge listed. He has stopped going to community gatherings; the press of a crowd makes his chest tighten, his breath catch. His wife says he is a ghost in his own house. When his grandchildren try to climb into his lap, he feels a distant, theoretical love, but the warmth of it seems to stop somewhere in his chest, unable to reach him fully. At night, he doesn’t sleep. He sits in the dark living room, listening to the house settle, waiting for a bell that will never ring again.
